clue.text: Space not to be confused with one of one's own

definitions.text: Space not to be confused with one of one's own

parts.words: Space not to be confused with one of one's own
parts.note: a Virginia Woolf title naming a room, not to be mixed up with her essay A Room of One's Own

explanation.surface: A warning not to mistake one kind of space for a private one.
explanation.walkthrough: Woolf wrote both a novel with a room in its title and the essay A Room of One's Own; 'Space' is the room, and the clue asks for the other one.
explanation.definitionFit: Woolf's 1922 novel takes its title from the young man's lodgings, a space distinct from the essay's private room.

clue.text: Leo Rosten happily shared those of yiddish

definitions.text: Leo Rosten happily shared those of yiddish

parts.words: Leo Rosten happily shared those of yiddish
parts.note: Leo Rosten's popular lexicon of Yiddish words carries a title about the pleasures of the language

explanation.surface: A writer cheerfully passing on the delights of a language.
explanation.walkthrough: Leo Rosten's 1968 book is The Joys of Yiddish; 'happily' hints at the pleasures in the title.
explanation.definitionFit: The pleasures or delights of Yiddish are what Rosten's book title promises.

clue.text: Old Fabian King?

parts.note: G. D. H. ... was a leading Fabian socialist, and 'Old King' points to the nursery-rhyme monarch who was a merry old soul

explanation.surface: A question about some elderly Fabian monarch.
explanation.walkthrough: The Fabian Society is a British socialist think tank; G. D. H. Cole was one of its leading figures. Read 'Old ... King' together and you get the nursery rhyme's Old King Cole.
explanation.definitionFit: The economist and historian G. D. H. Cole was a prominent Fabian, sharing a surname with the rhyme's merry monarch.

clue.text: Dowling boded no good in Lorca piece

indicators.note: the words are no good as written, so their letters must be reworked into something else

explanation.surface: Someone called Dowling had a bad feeling about a Lorca play.
explanation.walkthrough: 'no good' signals rearranging DOWLINGBODED.
explanation.definitionFit: Federico García Lorca's 1932 tragedy is set around a bride who runs off on her wedding day.

clue.text: Switched-on type in Capek piece

parts.note: Karel Čapek's play R.U.R. introduced the word for a manufactured worker, a machine one switches on

explanation.surface: A bright, alert character appears in a Czech play.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Switched-on' usually means clever and alert; here it means literally powered up. Čapek's 1920 play R.U.R. gave English the word for an artificial worker.
explanation.definitionFit: Čapek's play coined the term for a mechanical man, the kind of being that runs once switched on.

clue.text: They all informed against Hamlet, spurring his revenge

definitions.text: They all informed against Hamlet, spurring his revenge

parts.words: They all informed against Hamlet, spurring his revenge
parts.note: echoes Hamlet's soliloquy line 'How all ... do inform against me, And spur my dull revenge!'

explanation.surface: A group of informers betrayed Hamlet and drove him to vengeance.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue paraphrases Hamlet Act 4 scene 4: 'How all occasions do inform against me, And spur my dull revenge!' It reads as if people turned informer.
explanation.definitionFit: In the soliloquy the events and opportunities around Hamlet are what reproach him and goad him to act.

clue.text: He appears in some wild story, they say, about a ghost

definitions.text: He appears in some wild story, they say, about a ghost

parts.words: He appears in some wild story, they say, about a ghost
parts.note: 'wild story, they say' sounds like a Wilde story, here The Canterville Ghost, where the American minister Hiram B. is the head of the family

explanation.surface: Someone features in a far-fetched tale about a ghost.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wild', heard, is Oscar Wilde, and his story about a ghost is The Canterville Ghost, in which an American family moves into a haunted English house.
explanation.definitionFit: Hiram B. Otis is the American minister whose family buys Canterville Chase in Wilde's story.

clue.text: Cut scene of Jelly Roll Morton's early success

definitions.text: scene of Jelly Roll Morton's early success

explanation.surface: A slice of a jazz pianist's early career.
explanation.definitionFit: A choice cut of beef from the loin, and also the name of the red-light district where the jazz pianist Jelly Roll Morton first made his name.

clue.text: A visit … which the squire made on his horse with a pair of ——' containing his wardrobe " (Thomas Hughes)

definitions.text: A visit … which the squire made on his horse with a pair of ——' containing his wardrobe " (Thomas Hughes)

parts.words: A visit … which the squire made on his horse with a pair of ——' containing his wardrobe " (Thomas Hughes)
parts.note: a gap in a quotation from Tom Brown's Schooldays, filled by the pouches slung either side of a horse to carry clothes

explanation.surface: A quotation about a country squire riding off with his clothes packed on his horse.
explanation.walkthrough: Thomas Hughes wrote Tom Brown's Schooldays; the missing word names the paired bags that hang over a horse's back.
explanation.definitionFit: Paired pouches hung across a horse behind the rider are what would carry a travelling squire's clothes.

clue.text: Cowardly defender of cheap edition

parts.note: yellow is slang for lacking courage
a back is a defending player in football or rugby

explanation.surface: A timid full-back fond of bargain paperbacks.
explanation.definitionFit: Victorian railway-station novels were sold cheaply in yellow board covers, giving them their name.

clue.text: Seen with Miss Bagnold, returning to eat

indicators.note: coming back, so the word for eating is read from its last letter to its first

parts.note: to dine is to eat a meal

explanation.surface: A Miss Bagnold is spotted coming back for a meal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'returning' turns DINE around to ENID. 'Seen with' just joins the definition to the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: The author of National Velvet was Enid Bagnold, so her first name is the one wanted.

clue.text: "A good editor is a man … who has a — on my publisher" (John Cheever)

definitions.text: "A good editor is a man … who has a — on my publisher" (John Cheever)

parts.words: "A good editor is a man … who has a — on my publisher" (John Cheever)
parts.note: a gap in Cheever's quotation, filled by a wrestler's grip that leaves the opponent powerless

explanation.surface: John Cheever on the merits of an editor who can control a publisher.
explanation.walkthrough: Fill the dash with the word for a tight, controlling grip, from wrestling.
explanation.definitionFit: A grip round the neck that throttles, used figuratively for total control over someone.

clue.text: Poet is careless well edit this

indicators.note: the letters have been put down carelessly and must be set in their proper order

explanation.surface: A poet is told she has been sloppy and should polish this piece.
explanation.walkthrough: 'careless' signals rearranging WELLEDITTHIS; 'is' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Dame Edith Sitwell was an English modernist poet, author of Façade.

clue.text: Half a dozen of them looking for Pirandello?

definitions.text: Half a dozen of them looking for Pirandello?

parts.words: Half a dozen of them looking for Pirandello?
parts.note: Pirandello's play has six figures searching for an author, and Pirandello is himself an author

explanation.surface: Six people go searching for the Italian dramatist.
explanation.walkthrough: Pirandello's 1921 play is Six Characters in Search of an Author; since Pirandello is an author, the six could be looking for him.
explanation.definitionFit: The six people of Pirandello's play are figures in a story who seek someone to write them.

clue.text: Married woman, superb that is as bishop's wife

parts.note: Mrs is the title of a married woman
proud can mean splendid or magnificent
i.e. abbreviates id est, Latin for that is

explanation.surface: A married woman, magnificent, as befits the wife of a bishop.
explanation.walkthrough: 'as' is a link. Mrs Proudie is the domineering wife of Bishop Proudie in Trollope's Barchester novels.
explanation.definitionFit: In Trollope's Barchester Towers the overbearing spouse of the bishop of Barchester is the famous Mrs Proudie.

clue.text: He pressed his suit with white Italian girl in Padua

definitions.text: He pressed his suit with white Italian girl in Padua

parts.words: He pressed his suit with white Italian girl in Padua
parts.note: in The Taming of the Shrew a suitor in Padua woos Bianca, whose name is Italian for white

explanation.surface: A man ironing his suit with a pale Italian woman in Padua.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pressed his suit' means courted, not ironed; 'white Italian girl' is Bianca, Italian for white, the younger sister in The Taming of the Shrew.
explanation.definitionFit: Hortensio is one of Bianca's suitors in Padua, disguising himself as a music teacher to woo her.

clue.text: He pants, that is odd, for Alan Paton's neurotic aunt

indicators.note: the letters are in an odd, unusual order and need rearranging

parts.note: i.e. abbreviates id est, Latin for that is

explanation.surface: A man breathing heavily, which is strange, on account of an aunt in Paton's fiction.
explanation.walkthrough: 'that is' reads as part of the sentence but gives the Latin abbreviation; 'for' is a link. Alan Paton was the South African author of Too Late the Phalarope.
explanation.definitionFit: The setter identifies this character in Paton's fiction as the nervy, anxious aunt of the title.

clue.text: It came from the performer's cuff

definitions.text: It came from the performer's cuff

parts.words: It came from the performer's cuff
parts.note: something said off the cuff is improvised, so a performer's improvised line comes from the cuff

explanation.surface: Something a performer pulled from a shirt sleeve.
explanation.walkthrough: 'off the cuff' means without preparation, so the line that comes from a performer's cuff is an improvisation.
explanation.definitionFit: An improvised remark or passage, made up on the spot rather than scripted, is what comes off the cuff.

clue.text: "This particularly—, unintelligible patter" (W. S. Gilbert)

parts.note: the patter trio in Ruddigore describes its own breakneck song, and the gap wants a word for very fast

explanation.surface: Gilbert describing a fast, garbled patter song.
explanation.walkthrough: From Gilbert and Sullivan's Ruddigore: 'This particularly rapid, unintelligible patter Isn't generally heard, and if it is it doesn't matter.'
explanation.definitionFit: A patter song sung at great speed is quick, which suits the missing adjective.

clue.text: Casual departure of Marryat hero?

explanation.surface: A relaxed exit by the hero of a sea novel.
explanation.walkthrough: Captain Marryat's novel Mr Midshipman Easy has Jack Easy as its hero; his going would be his departure.
explanation.definitionFit: Relaxed and informal in manner, and read as two words, the leaving of Marryat's midshipman.

clue.text: Unreliable counsel shows 12 verses

indicators.note: advice that is unreliable cannot be trusted as given, so its letters are reworked

explanation.surface: Untrustworthy advice is revealed by a dozen lines of verse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Unreliable' signals rearranging COUNSELSHOWS. '12' refers to the answer at 12 across, the poet.
explanation.definitionFit: The poet at 12 across published her collection Clowns' Houses in 1918, so the title names a book of her poems.

clue.text: The world of Reginald Hill

parts.note: Reginald Hill wrote a Dalziel and Pascoe novel titled ..., so the word placed before 'world' makes his title

explanation.surface: An invitation into the universe of a crime novelist.
explanation.walkthrough: Reginald Hill's 1988 Dalziel and Pascoe mystery is Underworld; the answer is the word that goes with 'world' to make it.
explanation.definitionFit: Hill's novel title joins this word to 'world', making the criminal milieu his detectives investigate.

clue.text: Strange case of a rune

indicators.note: strange suggests something out of its normal form, so the word is rearranged

explanation.surface: An odd instance of an ancient letter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Strange' signals rearranging CASE; 'of' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: The Anglo-Saxon runic letter named for the ash tree, later written as the ligature æ.

clue.text: Poet of the riverbank

parts.note: a poet named Henry shares his surname with the tall grass that grows at the water's edge

explanation.surface: A versifier who writes about life by the river.
explanation.walkthrough: Henry Reed wrote the war poem Naming of Parts; the same word is a water plant of riverbanks.
explanation.definitionFit: The poet Henry Reed shares a name with the tall grass that lines rivers.

clue.text: Mythological stories from collected Danish lore

definitions.text: Mythological stories from collected Danish lore

indicators.note: the answer is taken from inside the words that follow

explanation.surface: Old myths drawn from a gathering of Scandinavian traditions.
explanation.walkthrough: 'from' points inside 'collectED DAnish'. The whole clue also describes the Old Norse collections of myth.
explanation.definitionFit: The Old Norse compilations of myth and heroic poetry gather the lore of the Norse peoples.

clue.text: Emergent Olympian swimmer

parts.note: the Greek epithet of Aphrodite as she rises from the sea, an Olympian goddess emerging from the water

explanation.surface: A rising star among Olympic swimmers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Olympian' suggests the Games, but means a god of Olympus: Aphrodite, painted rising from the waves, carries the Greek epithet meaning 'rising up'.
explanation.definitionFit: The Greek epithet means 'emerging from the sea', applied to Aphrodite born from the foam.

clue.text: Unwillingly introduce that of Pearl Buck

definitions.text: Unwillingly introduce that of Pearl Buck

parts.words: Unwillingly introduce that of Pearl Buck
parts.note: To drag something in is to introduce it unwillingly, so the title reads as drag on plus the answer

explanation.surface: An instruction to bring up something about the novelist reluctantly.
explanation.walkthrough: Pearl Buck's 1942 novel is Dragon Seed; 'Unwillingly introduce' points at dragging, the first part of the title.
explanation.definitionFit: The second word of Buck's novel title Dragon Seed, the source from which growth comes.

clue.text: Printed conceivably proud creed

indicators.note: conceivably means the letters could be put together in some other way

explanation.surface: A proud creed that might have been put into print.
explanation.walkthrough: 'conceivably' signals rearranging PROUDCREED.
explanation.definitionFit: Something printed has been copied out mechanically in multiple copies.
